name: Redensyl
lead: Redensyl is a patented cosmetic active ingredient for anti-hair-loss serums and lotions, developed by Givaudan Active Beauty (formerly Induchem). According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, it combines a larch-derived dihydroquercetin glucoside, a green tea derivative (EGCG2), glycine and zinc chloride, and is used at roughly 1 to 3 percent. [1]

The manufacturer-style claim is that it reactivates dormant hair follicle stem cells; the supporting data described in that source are in vitro or ex vivo. [1] Published human studies are small and typically test finished products that contain Redensyl together with other actives, often with industry-linked authors. [2][3][4]
Redensyl is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so products carrying it are not approved to treat hair loss. [1]
infobox: Dihydroquercetin glucoside, EGCG2, glycine, zinc chloride [1]
Cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug [1]

paras: Redensyl is sold to cosmetic manufacturers as a proprietary blend rather than a single molecule. Grokipedia describes the main active as dihydroquercetin glucoside, with the exact ratios proprietary. [1]

The claimed mechanism is stimulation of hair follicle stem cells and outer root sheath cells, with increased proliferation markers and Wnt pathway activity. The same source says these results come from cell culture and ex vivo follicle experiments and have not been directly shown to apply in living scalps. [1]

Grokipedia lists dihydroquercetin glucoside from larch extract and EGCG glucoside from green tea as the patented components, with glycine, zinc chloride and supporting agents, and describes the target cells as outer root sheath stem cells and follicular dermal papilla cells.[1] The ingredient is sold as a blend to formulators and appears in serums, lotions and shampoos, usually alongside other actives.[1][5]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source whose claims are unverified, states that Redensyl was developed by Induchem, a Swiss cosmetic-ingredient company, and introduced in February 2014 as the first cosmetic active designed to target hair follicle stem cells, with the trademark filed in March 2014 and registered in August 2015.[1] It says the ingredient received an innovation award at the in-cosmetics trade event in Hamburg and that Givaudan acquired Induchem in August 2015, bringing Redensyl into the Givaudan Active Beauty portfolio.[1]

The same source repeats manufacturer-reported figures, including an ex vivo follicle-culture result at 1 percent concentration and clinical data of new hairs after about three months, which are company-presented results rather than independent trials.[1] Redensyl later became a common label claim in direct-to-consumer hair serums, including rosemary-based products studied in 2025.[6]

A 2020 randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study randomized 44 people with androgenetic alopecia to a lotion containing Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 or a vehicle, twice daily for 24 weeks. Its authors reported improvements in investigator-assessed outcomes and the anagen-to-telogen ratio in the active group, with no significant adverse events. [2] The tested product combined two actives, so effects cannot be assigned to Redensyl alone. In that trial 41 of 44 patients (18 men, 23 women) completed it; among the 26 on the active lotion, 7.7 percent had great improvement, 73.1 percent moderate improvement and 19.2 percent stayed stable, the anagen-to-telogen ratio rose from 2.25 to 4.00 to 6.02 at weeks 0, 12 and 24, and self-assessment and quality-of-life scores improved.[2]

A 2024 study of 32 adults used a serum containing Redensyl, AnaGain, Procapil and other ingredients daily for 60 days; the authors reported increased hair growth rate and no adverse events. [3] A 2025 open-label, single-arm study of a rosemary and Redensyl serum in women over 120 days reported improvements across several measures, with no adverse effects. [6] The latter two studies had no control group in the abstracts described and were conducted by authors affiliated with a contract research firm and, in one case, the product company. In the 2024 study of 32 healthy adults aged 18 to 45, the authors reported hair growth rate up 10.52 percent at 30 days and 31.62 percent at 60 days, with density and thickness improvements.[3] The 2025 study tested a serum with rosemary, rice water, chia seed extract, Redensyl and other actives in an open-label design, and also measured graying.[6]

A 2023 randomized trial of 54 men compared platelet-rich plasma plus topical Procapil with platelet-rich plasma plus a Redensyl, saw palmetto and biotin product; the AGA grade differed significantly between groups in favour of the Redensyl combination. [4] A 2025 review of topical hair products discusses Redensyl among 'hyped' ingredients and weighs the clinical evidence available. [5]

A 2025 review of topical hair-growth actives, including Redensyl, Procapil, Capixyl, Baicapil, AnaGain, onion juice, coffee extract, saw palmetto, pumpkin seed oil and rosemary oil, looked at 24 articles and technical files. It reported promising results in randomized and cohort studies but noted limited sample sizes, no comparison with standard therapies, non-uniform groups, undisclosed alopecia type and conflicts of interest, and suggested these topicals might serve as add-on or alternative options.[5] No head-to-head trial of Redensyl against minoxidil in people was found.

Studies above report no significant adverse events, although they were short and small. [2][3][6] Grokipedia says Redensyl is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient in the EU and US, so labels cannot make medical claims, and that people with plant allergies are advised to patch-test. [1]

Redensyl is marketed as a non-hormonal, plant-based alternative to synthetic drugs, appealing to people who want to avoid finasteride or minoxidil side effects.[1] The 2025 trichology review describes sponsored social-media marketing of topical hair actives, and says serums have flooded the cosmeceutical market.[5]

timeline.event: Induchem introduces Redensyl as a cosmetic hair active, per Grokipedia.[1]
A randomized vehicle-controlled study of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion in 44 AGA patients is published.[2]
A 54-man randomized comparison of PRP with Procapil versus PRP with a Redensyl blend is published.[4]
A review weighs evidence for topical hair actives including Redensyl.[5]

lore.intro: Redensyl appears in hair-loss discussions as a serum ingredient pitched as a non-hormonal route to thicker hair.[1][5]

claims.claim: Redensyl reactivates dormant hair follicle stem cells
claims.believers: The developer-style description says the blend stimulates outer root sheath and dermal papilla cells and was tested in ex vivo follicle culture.[1]
claims.experts: The supporting data described are in vitro or ex vivo; the 2025 review describes the clinical evidence as mostly small studies of combined formulations.[1][5]

claims.believers: Company-reported ex vivo data described by Grokipedia claim it outperformed minoxidil in follicle culture.[1]
claims.experts: No head-to-head human trial against minoxidil was found; studies compare blends with vehicles or other topicals.[2][4][5]

claims.believers: Marketing and small studies report no significant adverse events.[2][3][6]
claims.experts: The studies were short and small, and Grokipedia advises patch-testing for people with plant allergies.[1]

card.summary: A patented plant-and-zinc blend in anti-hair-loss serums; small, industry-linked product studies, no approved-drug status.
card.note: Human studies tested multi-ingredient products, not Redensyl alone.

quick.overview:
Redensyl is a cosmetic ingredient used in over-the-counter hair serums. Its maker says it reactivates dormant follicle stem cells.

Small studies of products containing it report improvements, but they test blends, are short, and often have industry-linked authors.
quick.mechanism: Claimed to stimulate follicle stem and outer root sheath cells via Wnt-related signalling; support described is from lab and ex vivo work.
quick.risks: Reported adverse events in the small studies were none significant. It is a cosmetic, not an approved hair-loss drug; allergy patch-testing is advised for plant-sensitive people per Grokipedia.

chain: Serum or lotion applied to the scalp
Patented plant-and-zinc blend claimed to act on follicle stem cells and dermal papilla cells
angle.text: People apply Redensyl-containing serums to thinning areas hoping for fuller-looking hair, often as a non-hormonal add-on to other routines. Small product studies report better hair-growth measures, though they tested blends rather than Redensyl alone.[2][3][6]
